Python environments::Platform markers.summary: Use PEP 508 environment markers to make uv dependencies conditional on Python versions, operating systems, architectures, or other environment properties. Markers can also restrict dependency sources.
Python environments::Platform markers.explanation: Environment markers attach conditions to dependency declarations. uv evaluates markers such as the operating system or Python version and includes the dependency only when the condition matches; marker expressions can also be used to select dependency sources.

parameters.name: requirement
parameters.description: A dependency requirement followed by a PEP 508 environment marker expression.

parameters.name: environment marker
parameters.description: The marker expression, such as sys_platform == 'linux' or python_version < '3.9'.

Python environments::Platform markers.returns: The dependency is included only when its environment marker evaluates true for the target environment.

example.title: Linux-only dependency
example.code: uv add "jax; sys_platform == 'linux'"
example.explanation: Adds JAX only when the environment reports Linux.

useCases.title: Operating-system-specific dependency
useCases.scenario: A library is needed only on Linux.

useCases.title: Python-version-specific dependency
useCases.scenario: Different package releases support different Python versions.

useCases.title: Conditional dependency source
useCases.scenario: A package source or index should apply only to selected platforms.

The marker expression determines whether uv uses the requirement in the current environment.
Markers support operating system, architecture, Python version, and implementation conditions.
Use uv's alternate-platform and alternate-version options when checking or compiling for another target.
gotchas: Use a quoted requirement when adding a dependency with a marker, so the shell does not interpret the semicolon.
A universal resolution must remain installable across the project's complete requires-python range.

Python environments::Python installation.summary: Install supported Python interpreters with uv and understand the difference between uv-managed versions and system installations. uv can select existing interpreters or download compatible managed versions as needed.
Python environments::Python installation.explanation: uv can discover Python installations already on the system and can also download and manage supported CPython or PyPy distributions. It normally uses managed interpreters when available and downloads one automatically when needed; flags let you require managed or system interpreters.
Python environments::Python installation.syntax:
uv python install [TARGETS]
uv python list [--managed-python|--no-managed-python]

parameters.name: TARGETS
parameters.description: Python version or versions to install; if omitted, uv uses its configured version sources.

example.title: Install and select a managed interpreter
example.code:
uv python install 3.12
uv python list
uv run --python 3.12 python --version
example.explanation: Install a managed Python, inspect available interpreters, then run Python with the requested version.

useCases.title: Install a reproducible interpreter
useCases.scenario: A project requires a Python version that is not installed locally.

useCases.title: Require uv-managed Python
useCases.scenario: A command must not depend on operating-system or pyenv interpreters.

useCases.title: Use system Python only
useCases.scenario: An organization standardizes on an existing interpreter already available on each machine.

interview.question: How does uv distinguish managed and system Python?
interview.answer: uv recognizes interpreters already available on the machine as system Python installations. Versions downloaded by uv are managed Python installations; operating-system and pyenv installations remain system installations in uv's terminology.
interview.followUp: How can a command require one category? Use --managed-python to exclude system interpreters, or --no-managed-python to exclude managed interpreters.

interview.question: How do you install a specific Python version?
interview.answer: Run `uv python install` with a version such as `3.12` to install a managed interpreter. uv supports downloadable CPython and PyPy distributions for macOS, Linux, and Windows.
interview.followUp: What happens if no version is specified? uv verifies that a managed version is installed or installs the latest version.

interview.question: What is uv's default interpreter-selection behavior?
interview.answer: By default, uv attempts to use Python versions found on the system and downloads a managed version only when necessary. The `--managed-python` flag changes this behavior so system versions are ignored.
interview.followUp: How would you inspect only managed interpreters? Run `uv python list --managed-python`.

keyPoints: uv calls interpreters it downloaded and installed managed Python installations.
Every interpreter not installed by uv is classified as a system Python installation.
Supported managed distributions include CPython and PyPy across the three listed operating systems.
Interpreter selection prefers usable system versions before downloading a managed one.
A version can be installed explicitly with `uv python install`, followed by the requested version.
The --managed-python flag restricts selection to uv-managed interpreters.
gotchas: uv classifies Python installed by tools such as pyenv as system Python, not managed Python.
An explicit installation command is optional because uv can download a required version automatically.
Use --no-managed-python when the command must avoid uv-managed interpreters.

Python environments::Python version pinn.summary: uv lets a project declare its supported Python range with requires-python and record an interpreter preference. The range governs compatibility and dependency resolution, while the preference guides which Python installation uv selects.
Python environments::Python version pinn.explanation: uv records a project interpreter preference in the project configuration and uses the project's requires-python constraint when selecting a compatible interpreter. The preference controls whether uv uses managed or system Python installations, while requires-python defines the supported version range for the project and influences dependency resolution.

parameters.name: project.requires-python
parameters.description: Python version range supported by the project; declared under [project].

parameters.name: tool.uv.python-preference
parameters.description: Interpreter-selection policy controlling uv's preference for managed or system Python installations.

parameters.name: --python
parameters.description: Explicit interpreter or Python version for an individual command.

example.title: Declare support and select managed Python
example.code:
[project]
name = "example"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"

[tool.uv]
python-preference = "only-managed"
example.explanation: This project declares Python 3.12 or newer as supported, while uv is configured to prefer only uv-managed interpreters.

useCases.title: Standardize interpreter selection
useCases.scenario: A team needs reproducible local setup behavior.

useCases.title: Declare compatibility
useCases.scenario: A package supports several Python minor versions.

useCases.title: Constrain dependency resolution
useCases.scenario: A project resolves dependencies for multiple supported Python versions.

interview.question: How do you declare the Python versions a uv project supports?
interview.answer: Set the project's supported range with project.requires-python in pyproject.toml. uv uses that range when selecting compatible dependencies and interpreters.
interview.followUp: What happens if a dependency does not support the whole range? uv must choose a dependency version compatible with the project's declared range; otherwise resolution fails.

interview.question: What is the purpose of a project interpreter preference?
interview.answer: python-preference configures whether uv prefers managed Python installations or system interpreters. It expresses interpreter-selection policy, while requires-python expresses project compatibility.
interview.followUp: How can a CI job use a different interpreter? Pass --python, which explicitly selects the interpreter for that command.

interview.question: How does requires-python affect dependency resolution?
interview.answer: The project's requires-python range affects both allowed Python syntax and dependency-version selection. During resolution, dependencies must be compatible with the entire declared range.
interview.followUp: Why can a broad range make resolution harder? Every selected dependency must remain installable across that full range, which can exclude newer package releases.

keyPoints: Declare the project's supported Python range with project.requires-python in pyproject.toml.
The requirement also limits which Python syntax the project may use.
uv uses the declared range when selecting dependency versions, so dependencies must support that range.
gotchas: requires-python is not merely an interpreter selection hint: it also constrains syntax permitted in the project.

Python environments::uv pip compile and.summary: Resolve requirements into pinned `requirements.txt` or `pylock.toml` output with `uv pip compile`, then use `uv pip sync` to make an environment match that output exactly.
Python environments::uv pip compile and.explanation: `uv pip compile` resolves direct requirements and their compatible transitive dependencies into a pinned `requirements.txt` or `pylock.toml`. `uv pip sync` then installs the file's complete dependency set and removes packages that are not listed, producing an environment that matches the compiled output.
Python environments::uv pip compile and.syntax:
uv pip compile [OPTIONS] <SRC_FILE|--group <GROUP>>
uv pip sync [OPTIONS] <SRC_FILE>

parameters.name: SRC_FILE|--group GROUP
parameters.description: Compile input file or dependency group; commonly a requirements input file or pyproject.toml.

parameters.name: -o, --output-file
parameters.description: Output path for the generated requirements.txt or pylock.toml.

parameters.name: --python-platform
parameters.description: Target platform for resolution.

parameters.name: --python-version
parameters.description: Target Python version for resolution.

parameters.name: --universal
parameters.description: Generate a universal resolution.

parameters.name: SRC_FILE
parameters.description: Input requirements.txt or pylock.toml file used for synchronization.

parameters.name: --strict
parameters.description: Warn when transitive dependencies are absent from the input file.

Python environments::uv pip compile and.returns: `uv pip compile` writes a pinned `requirements.txt` or `pylock.toml`; `uv pip sync` updates the environment to match that file and removes packages not listed.

example.title: Compile and synchronize a virtual environment
example.code:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
printf 'requests\n' > requirements.in
uv pip compile requirements.in -o requirements.txt
uv pip sync requirements.txt
python -c "import requests; print(requests.__version__)"
example.explanation: Creates an environment, resolves the input requirement into a pinned requirements file, then makes the environment match that file.

useCases.title: Create a pinned requirements file
useCases.scenario: A project has direct dependencies in requirements.in and needs reproducible installs.

useCases.title: Enforce environment reproducibility
useCases.scenario: A CI job or deployment environment must contain exactly the reviewed dependency set.

useCases.title: Generate a universal resolution
useCases.scenario: One dependency file must support multiple operating systems.

useCases.title: Use pylock.toml output
useCases.scenario: A team is migrating from requirements.txt to the standardized lock format.

interview.question: How do `uv pip compile` and `uv pip sync` differ?
interview.answer: `uv pip compile` resolves an input such as `requirements.in` or `pyproject.toml` into a pinned `requirements.txt` or `pylock.toml`. `uv pip sync` consumes that output and changes the environment to match it, including removing unlisted packages.
interview.followUp: What happens when the compiled file omits a transitive dependency? It is not installed; use a complete compile or export output, or use `--strict` to warn about missing transitive dependencies.

interview.question: When should sync be preferred over install?
interview.answer: `uv pip sync requirements.txt` treats the file as the authoritative environment specification and removes packages that are not listed. `uv pip install` is the alternative when existing extra packages should remain.
interview.followUp: How would you synchronize from the newer lock format? Pass the `pylock.toml` file directly to `uv pip sync`, such as `uv pip sync pylock.toml`.

interview.question: What controls the portability of a compiled resolution?
interview.answer: By default, the pip interface produces a platform-specific resolution. `uv pip compile --universal` can instead produce a requirements file containing markers for the platforms where dependencies apply.
interview.followUp: How can compilation target another platform and Python version? Combine `--python-platform` and `--python-version`, for example for Linux and Python 3.10.

keyPoints: Use `uv pip compile requirements.in -o requirements.txt` to resolve an input file into pinned output.
A `pyproject.toml` can be compiled directly, with the output written to a requirements or pylock file.
Choose sync when reproducibility requires the installed environment to correspond exactly to the compiled file.
Sync accepts either of the documented resolution-output formats.
gotchas: Sync is destructive toward packages absent from the input file; use `uv pip install` when extra packages should be retained.
The sync input must contain the transitive dependencies, normally because it was generated by `uv pip compile` or `uv export`.

Python environments::uv pip install.summary: Use `uv pip install` for pip-compatible package installation in an environment outside uv's project workflow. It installs into a selected virtual or non-virtual Python environment and supports packages, extras, editable installs, Git sources, and requirement files.
Python environments::uv pip install.explanation: `uv pip install` provides a pip-compatible way to add packages to an environment. By default, uv targets an active virtual environment or discovers a `.venv`; use `--python` for a specific interpreter or `--system` for the system interpreter.

parameters.description: Package requirements, requirement files, or project metadata to install.

parameters.name: --python
parameters.description: Select a specific Python interpreter and its environment.

parameters.name: --system
parameters.description: Install into the system Python environment.

parameters.name: --extra
parameters.description: Install optional dependencies declared by a project.

parameters.name: --all-extras
parameters.description: Install all optional dependencies.

Python environments::uv pip install.returns: Installs the requested packages into the selected Python environment.

example.title: Install a package in a virtual environment
example.code:
uv venv
uv pip install ruff
example.explanation: Creates a virtual environment, then installs Ruff into the environment selected by uv.

useCases.title: Manage an external environment
useCases.scenario: You have an existing virtual environment and want pip-compatible installation without changing project metadata.

useCases.title: Install package requirements
useCases.scenario: You need to add a package, version constraint, or optional extra directly.

useCases.title: Install from dependency files
useCases.scenario: You want to populate an environment from requirements or project metadata.

useCases.title: Install a local project editably
useCases.scenario: You need an editable local checkout during development.

interview.question: Which environment does `uv pip install` modify by default?
interview.answer: It installs packages using uv's pip-compatible interface. The default target is an active virtual environment or a `.venv` found in the current directory or a parent directory.
interview.followUp: How would you target a non-virtual environment? Use `--python /path/to/python`, or use `--system` to select the first Python interpreter on `PATH`.

interview.question: What is a typical setup for installing a package?
interview.answer: Run `uv venv` to create the environment, then invoke `uv pip install package`. uv automatically uses the newly created `.venv` when it is in the current directory.
interview.followUp: How can installation be directed to a particular environment without activation? Pass its interpreter path with `--python /path/to/python`.

interview.question: How can packages be installed from dependency files?
interview.answer: Use `-r requirements.txt` to install from a requirements file. The interface also accepts a `pyproject.toml` through `-r`, and supports optional dependencies with `--extra` or `--all-extras`.
interview.followUp: How can build isolation be bypassed for a package with problematic build requirements? Preinstall the build dependency, then run `uv pip install --no-build-isolation package`.

keyPoints: The command is intended to substitute for common pip-style installation workflows with minimal packaging changes.
An activated virtual environment takes precedence as the installation target.
If no environment is active, uv searches upward for a `.venv` directory.
Use `--python` when the target environment is identified by a Python executable.
A direct package install uses the package name, such as `uv pip install flask`.
Extras can be requested by adding the extra in brackets to the package requirement.

Python environments::Virtual environment.summary: uv isolates package installations in virtual environments and lets you choose the Python interpreter before creating one. It discovers activated or nearby environments by default, while --python and --system provide explicit targeting.
Python environments::Virtual environment.explanation: uv keeps package installations isolated by preferring an activated environment, then a nearby .venv or Conda environment. Use uv venv to create one and --python to choose the interpreter; uv can obtain a requested Python version if needed. For an explicit target, pass the environment's Python executable, while --system opts into modifying system Python.
Python environments::Virtual environment.syntax:
uv venv [OPTIONS] [PATH]
uv venv --python <PYTHON> [PATH]
uv pip install [OPTIONS] [<PACKAGE>...]

parameters.name: --python
parameters.description: Python version or executable path used to create or target the environment.

parameters.name: --system
parameters.description: Opt into installing into the system Python environment.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Path of the environment to create; defaults to `.venv` in the current directory.

Python environments::Virtual environment.returns: A created virtual-environment directory, or installed packages in the environment selected by the interpreter and discovery rules.

example.title: Create and target an environment
example.code:
uv venv --python 3.12
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python requests
example.explanation: Creates a .venv environment with Python 3.12, then installs requests into that environment by explicitly selecting its interpreter.

useCases.title: Project isolation
useCases.scenario: Create a clean project-local environment before installing dependencies.

useCases.title: Interpreter selection
useCases.scenario: Ensure a project uses a required Python release.

useCases.title: Explicit environment targeting
useCases.scenario: Install into an existing environment without activating it.

useCases.title: Intentional system installation
useCases.scenario: Use a system interpreter only for controlled administrative or container workflows.

interview.question: How do you create a virtual environment with a specific Python version?
interview.answer: uv creates an isolated environment with `uv venv`. The `--python` option selects the interpreter used to create it, such as `uv venv --python 3.11`; uv can install the requested version when necessary.
interview.followUp: How can an installation target a particular environment without activating it? Use `uv pip install --python /path/to/venv/bin/python ...`, which selects the environment through its interpreter.

interview.question: How does uv choose an environment for `uv pip install`?
interview.answer: For mutating commands, uv first checks an activated environment through `VIRTUAL_ENV`, then an activated Conda environment through `CONDA_PREFIX`, and finally a `.venv` in the current or nearest parent directory.
interview.followUp: What takes precedence over those discovered environments? An explicit `--python` path identifies the target interpreter directly.

interview.question: How do you intentionally install outside a virtual environment?
interview.answer: The `--system` flag explicitly permits installation into the system Python, while `--python` can target any environment associated with a specified executable, including a non-virtual environment. The default is designed to avoid unintended system modifications.
interview.followUp: Why is `--system` not generally preferred? System Python layouts and distribution patches vary, so installations can be unsupported or cause complications.

keyPoints: Virtual environments separate project packages from the base Python installation, reducing dependency interference between projects.
For environment-mutating commands, uv prioritizes activated virtual environments, activated Conda environments, then a nearby .venv.
Run `uv venv` to create the conventional `.venv` directory in the working directory.
The `--python` option makes the target explicit and can point to an interpreter belonging to a non-virtual environment.
Use `--system` only as an explicit opt-in when modifying the system interpreter is required.
uv is independent of the Python runtime, but it still needs an interpreter target for dependency installation and source builds.
gotchas: Without an activated or discoverable virtual environment, ordinary uv pip installs do not target system Python; use --system or --python explicitly when that is intentional.
System installation may fail or behave differently across operating systems and distributions, so prefer an isolated environment.
A nearby .venv can be selected automatically, so check the directory hierarchy when an install appears to target an unexpected environment.

Resolution & workspaces::Constraints and.summary: Constraints restrict the versions permitted by existing requirements; overrides replace declared requirements and can widen the allowed range. Neither mechanism adds an otherwise unrequested package, and overrides are intended as a last resort when dependency metadata is known to be incorrect.
Resolution & workspaces::Constraints and.explanation: A constraint adds an allowed-version restriction to the requirements already declared by direct or transitive dependencies, so it can only narrow resolution and does not introduce a package. An override instead replaces those declared requirements for the named package, allowing resolution to select versions that the original metadata would reject; it is intended as a last resort when the metadata is wrong but compatibility is known.

parameters.name: constraint-dependencies
parameters.description: Requirement entries that narrow versions during resolution without requesting installation.

parameters.name: override-dependencies
parameters.description: Requirement entries that replace declared requirements for matching packages during resolution.

example.title: Constraining versus overriding a dependency
example.code:
[project]
dependencies = ["a", "b"]

[tool.uv]
constraint-dependencies = ["c>=1.0,<2.0"]
override-dependencies = ["c>=2.0"]
example.explanation: This project narrows c with a constraint and then replaces constituent requirements for c with an override; use one strategy for a real project, not both together.

useCases.title: Narrow a transitive range
useCases.scenario: A transitive dependency has many acceptable releases, but a project needs a bounded range for compatibility or reproducibility.

useCases.title: Keep resolutions synchronized
useCases.scenario: A project must align resolution with versions selected by another environment or dependency set.

useCases.title: Bypass bad metadata
useCases.scenario: A dependency declares an upper bound that is known to be incorrect, blocking a compatible release.

useCases.title: Scope overrides with markers
useCases.scenario: Different override requirements target the same package under different dependency conditions.

interview.question: How do constraints differ from overrides?
interview.answer: Constraints are additive restrictions on the versions allowed by existing requirements. They cannot add a package to the resolution, and they only matter when that package is already requested directly or transitively.
interview.followUp: What should be used to remove an erroneous upper bound? Use an override, because it replaces the constituent package requirements and can expand the acceptable version set.

interview.question: When is a constraint appropriate?
interview.answer: Use a constraint when a transitive dependency must stay within a narrower version range or when a resolution should remain aligned with another set of versions. Define it through a constraints file or the project’s constraint-dependencies setting.
interview.followUp: Does the constraint itself install the package? No; another direct or transitive dependency must request it.

interview.question: When should an override be used?
interview.answer: Use an override only when the declared metadata leads to an unsuccessful or undesirable resolution and compatibility with the replacement requirement is known. Overrides replace the requirements declared by constituent packages rather than combining with them.
interview.followUp: What happens in a workspace? All workspace members must remain mutually compatible because uv resolves their dependencies together.

keyPoints: A constraint narrows the acceptable versions for a package.
Listing a package only as a constraint does not add it to the resolution.
Constraints are especially useful for controlling transitive dependencies.
Overrides replace a package’s declared dependency requirements to bypass a problematic resolution.
Use overrides only as a last resort when compatibility with the replacement is known.
Constraints narrow; overrides can widen the acceptable version set.
Project overrides are declared with tool.uv.override-dependencies.
gotchas: An override does not cause an otherwise unrequested package to be installed.
An unscoped override also affects direct requirements, not only transitive ones.
Multiple overrides for one package need distinct markers.

Resolution & workspaces::Dependency upgr.summary: Upgrade a selected dependency with `uv lock --upgrade-package` while preserving other locked versions where possible. Review the resulting uv.lock changes because compatible transitive dependencies may also be re-resolved.
Resolution & workspaces::Dependency upgr.explanation: uv normally prefers versions already recorded in uv.lock, so ordinary locking does not upgrade released packages. Use --upgrade-package to deliberately refresh one dependency while retaining other locked versions where possible; the resolver may still change transitive packages when needed to produce a compatible solution.
Resolution & workspaces::Dependency upgr.syntax:
uv lock --upgrade-package <package>
uv lock --upgrade-package <package>==<version>
uv lock --upgrade

parameters.name: package
parameters.description: Package name, optionally followed by `==<version>`, identifying the dependency to upgrade.

Resolution & workspaces::Dependency upgr.returns: Updates the project's uv.lock resolution; the page does not define a separate return value.

example.title: Upgrade one dependency and inspect the lockfile
example.code:
uv lock --upgrade-package requests
uv diff --from uv.lock --to uv.lock
example.explanation: Upgrade only requests within the project's constraints, then inspect the resulting lockfile changes before committing them.

useCases.title: Focused package upgrade
useCases.scenario: A security or bug-fix release is available for one direct dependency and unrelated packages should remain stable.

useCases.title: Exact-version upgrade
useCases.scenario: A team needs to move a dependency to a known compatible release.

useCases.title: Full lockfile refresh

interview.question: How do you upgrade one dependency without upgrading everything?
interview.answer: Use `uv lock --upgrade-package <package>` to request the latest compatible version of one package while retaining other locked versions where possible. The request is still bounded by the project's dependency constraints.
interview.followUp: What if the requested package's upgrade requires a transitive change? uv may update transitive versions as part of finding a compatible resolution; inspect the lockfile diff before accepting it.

interview.question: Why does running `uv lock` not automatically fetch every newest release?
interview.answer: A lockfile is preferred during resolution, so already locked versions generally remain selected. Versions change when constraints make the old selection invalid or when an upgrade is explicitly requested with `--upgrade`.
interview.followUp: How would you refresh every dependency instead? Run `uv lock --upgrade`, then review the complete lockfile change.

interview.question: How can you request a specific version?
interview.answer: The command `uv lock --upgrade-package <package>==<version>` targets a specific version. The chosen version must still satisfy the project's dependency constraints, including any upper bounds.
interview.followUp: What should be checked when pinning an exact version? Confirm that the constraint is compatible with all project requirements and review any resulting transitive resolution changes.

keyPoints: Run `uv lock --upgrade-package <package>` when you want a focused upgrade rather than a repository-wide refresh.
Use `uv lock --upgrade-package <package>==<version>` to deliberately target an exact release.
Without an explicit upgrade, uv changes a locked package only when the existing selection no longer satisfies project constraints.
The resolver keeps an upgrade inside the ranges declared by the project, including upper bounds.
Use `uv lock --upgrade` when the intended scope is every dependency rather than a selected package.
gotchas: An explicit upgrade cannot cross the version bounds declared by the project.
Other packages remain pinned preferentially, so upgrading one direct dependency does not mean every package moves to its newest release.
A newly released package is not selected automatically merely because the lockfile is being reused.

Resolution & workspaces::Editable instal.summary: uv installs a configured project in editable mode by default, making source changes immediately available during development. Use `--no-editable` to perform a non-editable installation for deployment-style validation.
Resolution & workspaces::Editable instal.explanation: With a build system configured, uv normally installs the project in editable mode, so source changes appear immediately in the environment. Use the non-editable option when you need an installation that does not depend on the original source tree, such as when checking a deployment artifact.

parameters.description: Synchronize the project environment, installing the project and dependencies according to the lockfile.

parameters.name: uv run
parameters.description: Run a command in the project environment, applying project installation behavior.

parameters.name: --no-editable
parameters.description: Disable editable installation for the project and workspace members.

uv sync
uv sync --no-editable
example.explanation: The first command installs the project for development; the second installs a non-editable copy for a deployment-style check.

useCases.scenario: Local development

useCases.title: Check a non-editable project installation
useCases.scenario: Deployment validation

useCases.title: Avoid dependence on the source checkout
useCases.scenario: Container builds

interview.question: What does uv do by default when syncing a project?
interview.answer: uv installs a project in editable mode by default when a build system is defined. This makes source changes immediately visible in the project environment instead of requiring a reinstall.
interview.followUp: How would you test an installation that does not rely on the source checkout? Run `uv sync --no-editable`, which installs the project non-editably.

interview.question: How do you opt out of editable mode?
interview.answer: Use `uv sync --no-editable` or `uv run --no-editable`. The flag switches the project from editable installation to non-editable installation, which is suitable for deployment-oriented checks.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful for a container build? It avoids making the deployed environment depend on the originating source directory.

interview.question: Why use editable mode during development but non-editable mode for deployment?
interview.answer: Editable mode exposes the project source directly to the interpreter, so edits are reflected without rebuilding and reinstalling the project. Non-editable mode instead installs a built distribution into the environment.
interview.followUp: What limitation remains for native extensions? Editing native code does not rebuild the extension before it is imported.

keyPoints: A configured project is editable by default, so development does not require reinstalling after ordinary source changes.
The development environment sees source edits immediately because uv uses editable installation.
Both synchronization and execution commands can disable editable installation with `--no-editable`.
The flag requests a normal installation rather than one linked to the source tree.
Non-editable mode is intended for deployment scenarios, including Docker image construction.
gotchas: Editable installation applies only when the project declares a build system; otherwise uv installs dependencies without installing the project.
Editable installs have limitations: the build backend must support them, and changes to native modules do not trigger recompilation before import.

Resolution & workspaces::Git and path de.summary: uv supports Git and path dependency sources through [tool.uv.sources]. Pin Git sources to a commit revision for reproducibility; path sources can point to local wheels, archives, or projects.
Resolution & workspaces::Git and path de.explanation: uv records non-registry dependencies in [tool.uv.sources]. A Git source can use a repository URL plus a branch, tag, or immutable revision; for reproducibility, use a commit revision. A path source points to a wheel, source archive, or directory containing pyproject.toml, and relative paths are resolved from the project directory.

example.title: Pin a Git dependency to a commit
example.code:
[project]
dependencies = ["httpx"]

[tool.uv.sources]
httpx = { git = "https://github.com/encode/httpx", rev = "<commit-hash>" }
example.explanation: Declare the package normally, then map it to a Git source pinned to an immutable commit revision.

useCases.scenario: A project depends on unreleased upstream code.

useCases.title: Link a local project
useCases.scenario: Several packages are developed together in one repository.

useCases.title: Reproduce a fixed revision
useCases.scenario: A build must use an exact upstream snapshot.

interview.question: How do you declare a Git dependency in uv?
interview.answer: Use a Git source in [tool.uv.sources], such as { git = "https://...", rev = "<commit>" }. The project dependency remains named in [project.dependencies], while the source mapping selects the repository.
interview.followUp: How would you make a moving Git reference reproducible? Pin rev to a commit hash rather than relying on a branch or tag.

interview.question: What forms can a path dependency take?
interview.answer: A path source can reference a wheel, source distribution, or project directory. The path may be absolute or relative, and a project directory is built and installed by default.
interview.followUp: What must a directory path dependency contain? It needs a pyproject.toml so uv can treat it as a package.

interview.question: How do Git references affect reproducibility?
interview.answer: uv caches Git dependencies using the fully resolved commit hash, and compilation can write Git dependencies at a specific commit. Therefore, a commit-pinned source provides a clearer reproducibility strategy than an unpinned reference.
interview.followUp: What is the trade-off of a local path dependency in a lockfile workflow? Its contents are local and can change independently, so use a published or Git-pinned source when other environments need identical inputs.

keyPoints: Non-registry dependencies are configured through the project's [tool.uv.sources] mapping.
The documented source categories include index, Git, URL, and path.
Use git+ with HTTP(S) or SSH repository URLs when declaring a Git source.
A path dependency may target a wheel, source distribution, or local project directory.
Relative paths are supported, which is useful for sibling packages in a repository.
gotchas: A directory path is treated as an installable package by default; it must contain suitable project metadata.
Git command-line URLs need the git+ prefix when supplied as a dependency source.

Resolution & workspaces::Locked versus f.summary: Use --locked to reject a stale uv.lock instead of updating it. Use --frozen to use the existing lockfile without checking whether it matches current project metadata.
Resolution & workspaces::Locked versus f.explanation: uv normally checks and may update the lockfile before operations. Use --locked when the manifest and lockfile must already agree; use --frozen when the existing uv.lock should be used without checking whether it matches the project's current metadata.
Resolution & workspaces::Locked versus f.syntax:
uv run [OPTIONS] ...
uv run --locked ...
uv run --frozen ...
uv lock --check

parameters.name: --locked
parameters.description: Require the lockfile to be up-to-date; fail instead of updating it.

parameters.name: --frozen
parameters.description: Use the lockfile without checking whether it is up-to-date.

parameters.name: --check
parameters.description: Check whether the lockfile is up-to-date.

Resolution & workspaces::Locked versus f.returns: Commands succeed using the selected lockfile policy; --locked errors when the lockfile is stale, while --frozen errors when the lockfile is missing.

example.title: Compare lockfile modes
example.code:
uv run --locked python -c "print('validated')"
uv run --frozen python -c "print('lockfile used')"
example.explanation: The first command verifies that uv.lock is current and fails if it is not; the second uses the existing lockfile without checking it.

useCases.scenario: Continuous integration

useCases.title: Use a partial build context
useCases.scenario: Docker builds with only uv.lock mounted

useCases.title: Check lockfile freshness
useCases.scenario: Local validation

interview.question: When should --locked be used?
interview.answer: Use --locked when CI should reject a stale lockfile. uv checks that the lockfile is up-to-date and raises an error rather than updating it.
interview.followUp: What should be used when only uv.lock is available during an early Docker build? Use --frozen, because uv cannot validate the lock against project and workspace metadata that has not been copied yet.

interview.question: How does --frozen differ from --locked?
interview.answer: Use --frozen when the existing lockfile is the source of truth and uv must not check whether it is current. It still requires the lockfile to exist.
interview.followUp: What happens if uv.lock is absent? The command exits with an error instead of resolving dependencies.

interview.question: What is the practical distinction between the flags?
interview.answer: Both flags prevent the normal automatic lock update, but they enforce different guarantees: --locked validates freshness, while --frozen skips that freshness check.
interview.followUp: How can freshness be checked directly? Run uv lock --check, which is equivalent to --locked for other commands.

keyPoints: Use --locked to prevent automatic locking and require the committed lockfile to remain current.
A stale lockfile makes a --locked operation fail rather than silently rewriting uv.lock.
Use --frozen when you want uv to consume uv.lock without validating it against current metadata.
uv lock --check provides the direct freshness check corresponding to --locked on commands such as uv run.
gotchas: --frozen does not detect manifest changes or lockfile drift; it trusts the existing lockfile.
--locked fails when project metadata would require a lockfile update.

Resolution & workspaces::Lockfile export.summary: Export uv.lock into requirements.txt, pylock.toml, or CycloneDX v1.5 JSON when another tool cannot consume uv’s native lockfile. Choose the format with `--format` and save it with `--output-file`.
Resolution & workspaces::Lockfile export.explanation: `uv export` reads the project lockfile and converts its resolved dependencies into a format another tool can consume. Select `requirements.txt`, `pylock.toml`, or CycloneDX v1.5 with `--format`; use `--output-file` to save the result instead of printing it.

parameters.name: --format <format>
parameters.description: Selects the export format: requirements.txt, pylock.toml, or cyclonedx1.5.

parameters.name: --output-file <path>
parameters.description: Writes the export to the specified file instead of stdout.

parameters.name: --all-packages
parameters.description: Exports dependencies for all workspace members.

parameters.name: --locked / --frozen
parameters.description: Prevents uv from re-locking before export.

Resolution & workspaces::Lockfile export.returns: A serialized dependency export in the selected format, printed to stdout or written to the requested file.

example.title: Export for pip-based deployment
example.code:
uv export --format requirements.txt --output-file requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements.txt
example.explanation: Exports the uv lockfile as a pip-compatible requirements file, then installs that file with pip.

useCases.title: Generate requirements.txt
useCases.scenario: A deployment system accepts only pip-compatible dependency files.

useCases.title: Generate pylock.toml
useCases.scenario: A Python tool expects the standardized PEP 751 lockfile format.

useCases.title: Generate CycloneDX SBOM
useCases.scenario: Security or compliance tooling consumes software bill-of-materials data.

useCases.title: Export the whole workspace
useCases.scenario: A monorepo deployment needs dependencies from every workspace member.

interview.question: Why use uv export instead of consuming uv.lock directly?
interview.answer: `uv export` converts uv.lock into a format intended for another tool or workflow. The documented formats are requirements.txt, pylock.toml, and CycloneDX v1.5 JSON.
interview.followUp: How would you prevent export from changing resolution? Use `--locked` or `--frozen`, because the project is otherwise re-locked before exporting.

interview.question: How do you choose and save an export format?
interview.answer: Specify the target with `--format`, then use `--output-file` when the result must be written to disk. Without an output file, the export is printed to standard output.
interview.followUp: What happens if `--format` is omitted? uv defaults to requirements.txt, or infers the format from the output filename when one is provided.

interview.question: Which export formats does uv support, and when might they be used?
interview.answer: The `requirements.txt` output is compatible with pip-style installation workflows, while `pylock.toml` is the standardized Python lockfile format defined by PEP 751. CycloneDX output is intended for software-bill-of-materials workflows.
interview.followUp: How can a workspace export include every member? Add `--all-packages`; selected extras and groups then apply to all workspace members.

keyPoints: Use lockfile export when a deployment tool or workflow cannot consume uv.lock directly.
The documented export targets are requirements.txt, pylock.toml, and CycloneDX v1.5 JSON.
Pass `--format` to select the representation required by the downstream tool.
Without an output path, the generated content is emitted to standard output.
Use `--output-file` when deployment needs a generated artifact on disk.
A requirements.txt export can be installed by uv pip or pip.
gotchas: Do not generally maintain both uv.lock and requirements.txt as parallel sources of truth.

Resolution & workspaces::Package indexes.summary: Configure index order and authentication while keeping uv’s default first-index behavior, which limits resolution to the first index containing a package and reduces dependency-confusion risk.
Resolution & workspaces::Package indexes.explanation: uv consults configured indexes in declaration order, while the default PyPI index remains lowest priority. Its default first-index strategy stops considering candidates after the first index containing a package; authentication can be supplied through index configuration or supported credential sources, without switching to a strategy that combines candidates across indexes.

parameters.name: --index
parameters.description: Additional package index URL; repeated values are considered in order.

parameters.name: --index-strategy
parameters.description: Selects first-index, unsafe-first-match, or unsafe-best-match resolution behavior.

parameters.name: authenticate
parameters.description: Controls authentication behavior for a configured index.

example.title: Prioritize a private package index
example.code:
[[tool.index]]
name = "internal"
url = "https://packages.example.com/simple/"
explicit = true

[tool.uv]
index-strategy = "first-index"
example.explanation: Configure an internal index explicitly while retaining uv’s dependency-confusion-resistant default strategy.

useCases.title: Private plus public registries
useCases.scenario: A project uses an internal registry for proprietary packages and PyPI for public dependencies.

useCases.title: Dependency-confusion-resistant resolution
useCases.scenario: A build must ensure a package is selected from the first trusted index where it exists.

useCases.title: Authenticated package access
useCases.scenario: A registry requires a password or token and should have explicit per-index authentication behavior.

interview.question: How does uv prioritize multiple package indexes?
interview.answer: Indexes are searched in their configured order, with command-line indexes taking precedence over configuration-file indexes. The default PyPI index is special: it is always lowest priority.
interview.followUp: What happens when the same package exists on two indexes? With first-index, uv limits candidate versions to the first index where that package is found.

interview.question: Compare uv's index strategies.
interview.answer: first-index searches indexes in order and restricts resolution to the first index containing the package. unsafe-first-match and unsafe-best-match broaden selection across indexes, with unsafe-best-match exposing dependency-confusion risk.
interview.followUp: Why is first-index safer? A malicious package on another index cannot win merely by having a higher version when the package already exists on the preferred index.

interview.question: How does uv authenticate to package indexes?
interview.answer: Private indexes commonly require a username/password or access token. uv first tries an unauthenticated request, then searches for credentials and retries authenticated access when credentials are available; per-index authenticate settings can change this behavior.
interview.followUp: Where can credentials come from? Supported sources include the URL, netrc, uv's credential store, and optionally a keyring provider.

keyPoints: Declare private indexes before lower-priority sources when package ownership should prefer the private source.
Command-line index declarations override the corresponding ordering from configuration files.
PyPI is available implicitly unless the configuration changes the default-index setup.
The default resolver examines indexes in order and confines versions to the first matching index.
Authentication behavior can be customized for an individual index rather than applied only globally.
Private registries generally need basic credentials or an access token for package retrieval.
gotchas: Avoid unsafe-best-match unless you deliberately accept dependency-confusion risk; it combines candidates from all indexes.
Moving the default index in the configuration does not make it higher priority.
A failed unauthenticated request can trigger credential lookup, so configure the relevant authentication source rather than assuming credentials are sent first.

Resolution & workspaces::Workspace membe.summary: Resolve a multi-package workspace together with one shared lockfile, while using --package to choose which member uv run or uv sync targets.
Resolution & workspaces::Workspace membe.explanation: A workspace groups multiple Python packages under one root and gives them a shared lockfile. uv resolves the complete workspace together; commands such as uv run and uv sync default to the root, but --package lets you target a particular member from any workspace directory.
Resolution & workspaces::Workspace membe.syntax:
[tool.uv.workspace]
members = ["packages/*"]
exclude = ["packages/seeds"]

uv run --package <member> <command>
uv sync --package <member>

parameters.name: --package
parameters.description: Workspace member name passed to select the package targeted by uv run or uv sync.

parameters.name: members
parameters.description: Required list of globs identifying directories included as workspace members.

parameters.name: exclude
parameters.description: Optional list of globs identifying directories excluded from membership.

example.title: Define and target workspace members
example.code:
[tool.uv.workspace]
members = ["packages/*"]
exclude = ["packages/seeds"]

# From the workspace root:
# uv lock
# uv run --package api python -m api
# uv sync --package web
example.explanation: This workspace resolves all included packages together, while --package selects the member targeted by run or sync.

useCases.title: Coordinate monorepo dependencies
useCases.scenario: A monorepo contains several applications and libraries that must share a consistent dependency resolution.

useCases.title: Target one member
useCases.scenario: A developer needs to execute a command against one package without changing the current directory.

useCases.title: Filter workspace membership
useCases.scenario: A workspace uses broad directory globs but must omit generated or special-purpose projects.

interview.question: How does uv represent a workspace and resolve it?
interview.answer: A workspace is a group of packages managed together. Each package has its own pyproject.toml, while uv uses one lockfile for the workspace, so uv lock resolves the packages as a unit.
interview.followUp: How can one member depend on another? Declare the dependency with tool.uv.sources and set workspace = true for the member.

interview.question: How do you define which directories are workspace members?
interview.answer: Add a tool.uv.workspace table to pyproject.toml. The members key is required and accepts directory globs; exclude is optional and removes matching directories.
interview.followUp: What must each selected directory contain? A pyproject.toml file, otherwise it does not satisfy the workspace member requirement.

interview.question: How do you choose a particular member for commands?
interview.answer: uv run and uv sync target the workspace root by default. Pass --package with a member name to run or sync that member from any directory in the workspace.
interview.followUp: How do you inspect the workspace? Use uv workspace list for member names, or uv workspace dir --package NAME for a member path.

keyPoints: A workspace is a managed group of one or more packages called workspace members.
Members keep separate project metadata, but dependency locking is shared across the workspace.
Locking resolves the complete workspace rather than only the package where the command is run.
Run and sync use the root unless a different member is selected.
Use --package to target a named member for run or sync from anywhere within the workspace.
Workspace configuration requires members; exclude can narrow the included directories.
gotchas: All directories selected by members and not removed by exclude must contain their own pyproject.toml.
The root is always included as a workspace member, so it cannot be treated as an unrelated container.
When declaring a dependency on another member, use an explicit workspace source rather than relying on implicit discovery.

Tools & delivery::Cache management.summary: Inspect uv's cache separately from a project's declared dependencies, then measure, prune, or clear cached data. Package-specific cleaning, full cleaning, and CI-focused pruning support targeted maintenance without changing project dependency declarations.
Tools & delivery::Cache management.explanation: uv keeps disposable but reusable downloads, builds, and environments in a cache separate from the dependencies declared by a project. Use cache commands to locate or measure it, remove unused entries, clear selected packages, or empty it entirely; uv recreates needed environments and cache data later.
Tools & delivery::Cache management.syntax:
uv cache [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>
uv cache dir
uv cache size
uv cache clean [OPTIONS] [PACKAGE]...
uv cache prune [OPTIONS]

parameters.name: PACKAGE
parameters.description: Optional package names whose cache entries should be removed by `uv cache clean`.

parameters.name: OPTIONS
parameters.description: Optional command options controlling cache operations.

example.title: Inspect and prune uv's cache
example.code:
uv cache dir
uv cache size
uv cache prune
uv cache clean ruff
example.explanation: Inspect the cache location and size, remove unused entries, then optionally clear cached data for one package.

useCases.title: Find and reduce cache storage
useCases.scenario: Local maintenance

useCases.title: Invalidate one package's cached data
useCases.scenario: Targeted troubleshooting

useCases.title: Minimize retained CI cache data
useCases.scenario: Continuous integration

interview.question: How do you inspect and reduce uv's cache?
interview.answer: `uv cache dir` prints the active cache path, while `uv cache size` reports its size. `uv cache prune` removes unused entries and centralized project environments; `uv cache clean` removes all entries or entries for named packages.
interview.followUp: How would you reduce a CI cache after a job? Run `uv cache prune --ci`, which removes pre-built wheels and unpacked source distributions but keeps wheels built from source.

interview.question: How is uv's cache different from project dependencies?
interview.answer: The cache stores disposable data that improves reuse, not the project's declared dependency specification. Cleaning or pruning it does not edit project metadata; uv recreates needed cached environments and data when required.
interview.followUp: What happens to centralized project environments after pruning? They are removed and recreated as needed.

interview.question: How can you clear only one package's cached data?
interview.answer: Use `uv cache clean <package-name>` to invalidate cached data for one package, such as `uv cache clean ruff`. Use `uv cache clean` without a package to clear every cache entry.
interview.followUp: What remains after a full clean? The cache directory and its lock file remain so other uv processes can share the cache safely.

keyPoints: Run `uv cache dir` to discover which cache location the current uv invocation uses.
Pruning removes unused cache data and centralized project environments rather than declared project dependencies.
Pass one or more package names to clean cached entries associated with selected packages.
A package-less clean empties the cache contents completely.
Periodic pruning is an appropriate maintenance operation because it targets entries uv no longer needs.
gotchas: A full clean removes cache entries but leaves the cache directory and lock file in place.
In CI, the specialized prune mode removes pre-built wheels and unpacked source distributions while retaining wheels built from source.
Disabling caching does not mean uv has no cache directory: it uses a temporary directory for that operation.
For best performance, place the cache and virtual environments on the same filesystem.

Tools & delivery::Script metadata.summary: Declare a standalone Python script's dependencies in an inline TOML metadata block. uv reads the block when running the script and creates an environment with the required packages.
Tools & delivery::Script metadata.explanation: A standalone Python script can carry its own dependency declaration in a TOML metadata block at the beginning of the file. `uv run` reads that block, creates an isolated environment for the script, and installs the specified packages; `uv add --script` can create or update the declaration.

parameters.name: requires-python
parameters.description: Python version constraint for the script, such as `>=3.12`.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Packages required by the script, expressed as dependency specifiers.

example.title: Standalone script with inline dependencies
example.code:
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.12"
# dependencies = [
#   "requests<3",
# ]
# ///
import requests

print(requests.get("https://astral.sh").status_code)
example.explanation: Save as example.py and run it with `uv run example.py`; uv reads the embedded metadata and supplies the declared package.

useCases.title: Portable utilities
useCases.scenario: A single-file utility needs third-party packages but should not require a checked-in project.

useCases.title: Self-describing scripts
useCases.scenario: A script is shared with colleagues or executed on another machine.

useCases.title: Project-independent execution
useCases.scenario: A script needs a different dependency set from the project containing it.

interview.question: How does a standalone script declare dependencies?
interview.answer: Put a PEP 723-style TOML block at the top of the Python file, using fields such as `requires-python` and `dependencies`. Running the file with `uv run` causes uv to create an environment containing the declared packages.
interview.followUp: What happens if the file is run from a uv project? The script's inline dependency set is used and the project's dependencies are ignored.

interview.question: How can metadata be added or changed?
interview.answer: Use `uv add --script example.py package-specifier` to add or update the script's inline metadata. uv writes the dependency declaration into the script rather than requiring a separate project file.
interview.followUp: How would you add a package from another index? Supply the index with `--index` when invoking `uv add --script`.

interview.question: What is the required metadata shape?
interview.answer: The metadata uses a `script` block represented by TOML comments, and the `dependencies` field is required even when it is empty. This keeps the dependency information in the script itself.
interview.followUp: What benefit does this provide at execution time? uv can create the environment needed for that particular script on demand.

keyPoints: Dependencies travel with the script, so a standalone file can describe what it needs without a separate dependency manifest.
Use uv commands to maintain the embedded declaration instead of editing dependency entries manually.
`uv add --script file.py package` is the documented command pattern for adding packages.
Execution provisions an environment from the metadata when the script is run.
The format follows Python's standardized inline script metadata approach.
gotchas: The metadata block must include `dependencies`, including when the script currently has no packages.
Do not add `--no-project` merely to isolate a script that already declares inline metadata.

Tools & delivery::uv build.summary: `uv build` creates source and wheel distributions, normally under `dist/`. Inspect those archives to verify the files included before delivery.
Tools & delivery::uv build.explanation: Run `uv build` in a project directory to create distributions in `dist/`. uv first creates the source distribution, then builds the wheel from that source archive; use selection flags when only one format is needed. The build backend, rather than uv itself, determines package contents.

parameters.name: --sdist
parameters.description: Build only a source distribution.

parameters.name: --wheel
parameters.description: Build only a wheel distribution.

parameters.name: <SRC>
parameters.description: Build the package in the specified directory.

parameters.name: --package <PACKAGE>
parameters.description: Build the named package within the current workspace.

Tools & delivery::uv build.returns: Creates source and/or wheel distribution files in the `dist/` directory.

example.title: Build and inspect distributions
example.code:
uv build
python -m zipfile -l dist/*.whl
 tar -tzf dist/*.tar.gz
example.explanation: Build both distributions, then list their contents to verify which files were packaged.

useCases.title: Create release distributions
useCases.scenario: Prepare release artifacts for publishing to a package registry.

useCases.title: Audit packaged files
useCases.scenario: Check whether documentation, package modules, metadata, or other required files made it into the archives.

useCases.title: Select a distribution format
useCases.scenario: Generate only the artifact type required by a downstream release workflow.

interview.question: What does `uv build` do?
interview.answer: `uv build` acts as a PEP 517 build frontend: it selects the Python version and invokes the backend configured in `[build-system]`. By default it writes the generated artifacts to `dist/`.
interview.followUp: How would you build only one artifact? Use `--sdist` for a source distribution or `--wheel` for a wheel.

interview.question: What is the difference between an sdist and a wheel?
interview.answer: A source distribution contains source and metadata, while a wheel contains pre-built artifacts that can be installed directly. Running `uv build` creates both by default.
interview.followUp: Why inspect both? Their contents and installation paths can differ, so each should be validated before publishing.

interview.question: How do you verify what was packaged?
interview.answer: Use `uv build --sdist` or `uv build --wheel` to select one format, and inspect the resulting archive files under `dist/`. The backend determines which project files enter those archives.
interview.followUp: How can you test packaging completeness? Install or run smoke tests against each generated distribution in an isolated environment.

keyPoints: The command supports the two standard Python distribution formats: source archives and installable wheels.
With no path or package selector, it builds the current project and places the results in `dist/`.
Use `--sdist` when the delivery artifact should be only a source distribution.
Use `--wheel` to produce only the wheel artifact.
Passing both format flags explicitly builds both distributions directly from project source.
gotchas: Do not assume uv controls package contents or filenames; inspect the configured build backend when files are missing or unexpected.
The wheel is built from the generated source distribution, so testing the source archive helps catch omissions that could affect the wheel.

Tools & delivery::uv in CI.sourceTitle: Using uv with GitHub Actions | uv
Tools & delivery::uv in CI.summary: In CI, pin uv and Python, cache using the dependency lockfile, fail when uv.lock is stale, and synchronize without updating it. Prune the cache afterward to control its size.
Tools & delivery::uv in CI.explanation: In CI, install a known uv release and the project’s required Python version, then persist uv’s cache with a key derived from the lockfile. Check that uv.lock is current before using --locked synchronization, and prune the cache at the end to keep restored artifacts efficient.
Tools & delivery::uv in CI.syntax:
uv lock --check
uv sync --locked
uv cache prune --ci

parameters.name: version
parameters.description: Optional uv release to install; pin this in CI for repeatable tool behavior.

parameters.name: python-version
parameters.description: Python version used by the job or project; configure it explicitly or follow the project pin.

parameters.name: enable-cache
parameters.description: Enables persistence of uv’s cache across workflow runs.

parameters.name: cache-dependency-glob
parameters.description: Files used to determine cache invalidation; use uv.lock for project workflows.

Tools & delivery::uv in CI.returns: A CI job with a pinned uv tool and interpreter, dependency-aware cache restoration, stale-lockfile failure, reproducible synchronization, and CI cache cleanup.

example.title: Pinned uv CI job
example.code:
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v7
        with:
          version: "0.9.17"
          python-version: "3.12"
          enable-cache: true
          cache-dependency-glob: uv.lock
      - run: uv lock --check
      - run: uv sync --locked
      - run: uv run pytest
      - run: uv cache prune --ci
example.explanation: A GitHub Actions job pins uv and Python, keys its cache from uv.lock, rejects an outdated lockfile, installs without changing the lockfile, runs tests, and trims CI cache entries.

useCases.title: Reproducible tests
useCases.scenario: GitHub Actions test workflows

useCases.title: Faster dependency setup
useCases.scenario: Jobs that repeatedly install the same dependencies

useCases.title: Lockfile enforcement
useCases.scenario: Teams committing uv.lock

useCases.scenario: Large or frequent CI workloads

interview.question: How would you make uv-based GitHub Actions reproducible?
interview.answer: Use the official setup-uv action, set its version explicitly, enable caching, and configure the Python version. The action can install uv, place it on PATH, and persist the cache; project commands can then use uv sync and uv run.
interview.followUp: How should cache invalidation work? Include uv.lock in the cache key so dependency changes restore a compatible cache rather than reusing an unrelated one.

interview.question: How do you prevent stale dependency resolution in CI?
interview.answer: Run uv lock --check to fail when the committed lockfile is not up to date, then run uv sync --locked so synchronization cannot silently update it. This separates validation of the lockfile from installation.
interview.followUp: What changes for a uv pip workflow? Key the cache from requirements.txt rather than uv.lock, because uv pip does not use the project lockfile in that way.

interview.question: How should the uv cache be restored and maintained?
interview.answer: Enable the uv cache in the setup action and key it with the operating system plus a hash of uv.lock. Add a fallback operating-system key if desired, then run uv cache prune --ci after the job to reduce cache size.
interview.followUp: Why is pruning not guaranteed to speed every job? Its effect depends on the packages being installed, so retaining source-built wheels may be more valuable for some workloads.

keyPoints: Use the official setup action to install uv and expose it to subsequent job steps.
The setup action can follow the project’s Python pin instead of relying on the runner’s default interpreter.
Persisting the uv cache can reduce repeated package-download and build work.
Include the operating system and uv.lock hash in the cache key to restore dependency-compatible artifacts.
Prune the cache after the job to discard CI-unhelpful artifacts while retaining useful built wheels.
gotchas: Pruning is recommended, but its performance benefit depends on which packages the job installs.
The uv project workflow and uv pip workflow use different dependency files for cache invalidation.
When using the official setup action, avoid assuming the runner’s default interpreter matches the project pin.

Tools & delivery::uv in Docker.summary: Use Docker layer ordering and BuildKit cache mounts to make uv dependency installation reusable across builds. Copy metadata first, install dependencies without the project, then copy source and install the project.
Tools & delivery::uv in Docker.explanation: In a Docker build, copy only the project metadata and lockfile first, then run `uv sync --frozen --no-install-project` with a persistent BuildKit cache mount. Copy application files afterward and run `uv sync --frozen` to install the project without invalidating the dependency layer whenever source changes. Keep the environment inside the image rather than copying a host-created `.venv`.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: BuildKit cache mount target used for uv's cache.

parameters.name: --frozen
parameters.description: Prevents uv from changing dependencies or the lockfile.

parameters.name: --no-install-project
parameters.description: Skips installing the local project during the dependency layer.

Tools & delivery::uv in Docker.returns: A Docker image containing the locked dependencies and application virtual environment.

example.title: Cache uv dependencies in Docker
example.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim

COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:latest /uv /uvx /bin/

WORKDIR /app

# Install dependencies before copying application source.
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv \
    uv sync --frozen --no-install-project

# Copy source and install the project.
COPY . /app
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv \
    uv sync --frozen

CMD ["/app/.venv/bin/python", "-m", "myapp"]
example.explanation: This Dockerfile separates dependency installation from source copying and uses a BuildKit cache mount for uv's cache.

useCases.title: Reuse dependency layers
useCases.scenario: Application source changes frequently but dependency metadata is stable.

useCases.title: Persist uv's build cache
useCases.scenario: Repeated Docker builds need faster dependency installation.

useCases.title: Build the environment in Docker
useCases.scenario: A container image should contain its own environment rather than a host-created environment.

keyPoints: Mount uv's cache at `/root/.cache/uv` with Docker BuildKit so dependency artifacts can be reused between builds.
Install dependencies without installing the local project before copying source files, preventing source changes from invalidating that layer.
Set copy link mode when using a cache mount so the environment does not depend on links into the cache.
gotchas: Without a cache mount, use `--no-cache` when reducing the final image size matters.

Tools & delivery::uv publish.summary: Publish already-built Python distributions with `uv publish`. Use scoped credentials and a named index or upload URL so artifacts go to the intended registry.
Tools & delivery::uv publish.explanation: After distributions have been built, uv uploads them to a package registry. Credentials can come from command-line options or environment variables, while a configured named index provides a deliberate publishing target and its upload endpoint.

parameters.name: --password <password>
parameters.description: Provide the publishing password.

parameters.name: --publish-url <url>
parameters.description: Specify the upload endpoint.

parameters.name: --check-url <url>

parameters.name: --no-attestations

uv build
UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN="$PYPI_TOKEN" uv publish --index pypi

useCases.title: Private-index publishing

useCases.title: Credential-free trusted publishing
